## The question

Flood risk is usually mapped as a physical hazard, but the consequences of a
flood depend just as much on who lives in the flooded area. This project asks
where in London the two overlap: which neighbourhoods face both a high
probability of surface water flooding *and* a population least equipped to
recover from it.

## Data

| Source | Dataset | Geography |
|---|---|---|
| Environment Agency | Risk of Flooding from Surface Water | 2 m raster |
| ONS | Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019 | LSOA |
| ONS | Census 2021 population | LSOA |

: Datasets used in this analysis {.striped .hover}

## Method

The workflow was three steps: zonal statistics of the flood raster over LSOA
boundaries, a normalised vulnerability index from the IMD domains, and a
bivariate classification of the two.

```python
import geopandas as gpd
import rasterstats as rs

lsoa = gpd.read_file("data/lsoa_london.gpkg")
stats = rs.zonal_stats(
    lsoa,
    "data/rofsw_london.tif",
    stats=["mean", "max"],
    nodata=-9999,
)
lsoa["flood_mean"] = [s["mean"] for s in stats]
```

## Findings

Three points stood out:

1. Exposure is concentrated along the Lea Valley and in pockets of south-east London.
2. The correlation between flood depth and deprivation is weak overall, but the
   tail matters — 41 LSOAs sit in the top decile of both.
3. Those 41 LSOAs house roughly 78,000 people.

::: {.callout-note}
## Caveat
The surface water model does not account for drainage capacity upgrades made
after 2022, so risk in parts of Camden is likely overstated.
:::

## What I would do next

Add a temporal dimension using rainfall return periods, and test whether the
overlap holds when vulnerability is measured with health rather than income
indicators.
